item.title: Trump says Iran is making up strikes on ships to drive up oil prices
item.description:
What to know about the Iran war today: President Trump accused Iran of making up the fact that ships in the Strait of Hormuz are hitting mines or being struck by missiles or drones, saying it was a bid to drive up oil prices before the midterms.The price of Brent crude oil surged about 4% on Thursday to $113 per barrel as Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it had attacked four vessels near the Strait of Hormuz for using a route that Tehran rejects. The IRGC said three other ships using that route hit sea mines and were forced to halt.The U.S. military has quietly reduced its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing threats and attacks by Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, sources told CBS News on Wednesday. The latest attack, on King Fahd International Airport in the eastern Saudi city of Dammam, has killed at least two people and injured eight more.
New Updates
44m ago
U.S. celebrates 100 days since reinstating blockade on Strait of Hormuz
The U.S. Central Command posted a celebration Thursday of 100 days of its reinstated blockade on Iranian ships entering or exiting ports through the Strait of Hormuz.
The blockade has prevented $25 billion in crude oil exports by Iran, according to CENTCOM.
The blockade was reinstated on July 14 after the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding fell apart over the wording of one of the clauses. Iran believed it would determine navigation through the strait and withhold charging fees for at least 60 days. The U.S. said the wording in the memorandum did not allow for Iran to determine transit.

item.title: Zelenskyy accuses Russia of using cluster warheads in deadly strikes
item.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accused Russia of using cluster munitions overnight as it renewed strikes on Kyiv and multiple other locations.
At least four people were killed, according to Ukraine's foreign ministry. Another 34 people were injured, including five children, Zelenskyy said Thursday, hours after Russia released American Stephen Hubbard and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and called him a humanitarian.
"Last night, the Russians used, among other weapons against Kyiv, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads," Zelenskyy wrote on X Thursday. "The distinguishing feature of these missiles is that they detonate in the air as they approach the target, striking everything within a 400-meter diameter."
More than 100 countries have banned the use of cluster bombs under the Convention on Cluster Munitions, an international treaty that was adopted in 2008. The munitions spread smaller "bomblets" over a wide area that can hit civilian locations indiscriminately.
Russia, like the United States, did not sign on to the treaty.
A shopping mall stands damaged by a Russian missile strike on Oct. 22, 2026, in Kyiv, Ukraine.
Sofiia Lavska/Apostrophe/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images
Russia's Defense Ministry said, meanwhile, that air defenses downed 808 Ukrainian drones overnight, and that two people were reported injured, The Associated Press reported. More than 600 drones were fired toward Moscow between late Wednesday and early Thursday, according to Mayor Sergei Sobyanin.

item.title: WWII fighter plane wreckage, pilot's personal items found underground
item.description:
The wreckage of a World War II-era Soviet jet was discovered in rural Hungary, along with some of its pilot's personal items, according to the Hungarian Museum of Military History and local media.
Excavators unearthed the Soviet Yakovlev Yak-1 fighter aircraft from about 17 feet underground in the central Hungarian village of Törtel, which is located about 50 miles southeast of Budapest, museum officials said. István Kocsis, a member of the research association who led the investigation into the wreck, said excavations in the area began in September.
Several portions of the plane were relatively intact when archaeologists recovered them from the crash site. The relics included what officials identified as a piece of the red star insignia printed on all Soviet military properties at the time, which they said was "in relatively good condition."
Part of the aircraft's fuselage was also recovered, displaying the jet's side number, in addition to the pilot's personal belongings. Among them was a book containing the pilot's signature, which experts at the museum are currently working to restore, the museum said.
Some of the best-preserved pieces of the wreck will be exhibited by the military museum, once its archaeology department has finished carrying out restoration procedures and logged records of their obervations.
Although scientists and archaeologists alike are still working to learn more about the decades-old debris, they were able to trace the wreckage back to a particular wartime crash that took place in November 1944, Hungarian local media reported. While opposing each other over Törtel, German Lt. Peter Düttmann and Soviet Lt. Alexander Semyonovich Andrianov's aerial duel ended with Düttmann shooting down the Soviet aircraft. Although Andrianov escaped by parachute, he later became a prisoner of war, according to the news site Hungary Today.

item.title: Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield, and what they mean to Ukraine
item.description:
Over the past week, Ukraine has received a stark reminder of its growing dependence on uninterrupted access to Elon Musk's Starlink and Starshield networks in its drone-heavy war against Russia, now in its fifth year.
Ukraine has a fraction of Russia's resources, but its aggressive development of drone warfare on defensive and offensive fronts has helped it endure an onslaught from its much bigger adversary, which invaded Ukraine in early 2022. That was true until last week, when Ukraine reported a throttling of the Starshield network that was causing its drones to stop midflight and fall out of the sky.
The two SpaceX networks operate on a constellation of thousands of low-Earth satellites — Starlink is the commercial version, while Starshield is a military product licensed to the U.S. government and its partners, among them Ukraine.
Kyiv's reliance on drones has made Starlink and Starshield nearly indispensable to its arsenal. When Ukraine experienced a disruption to those networks, it lost the shield of interceptors and drones that offered some protection against Russian drone and missile strikes.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy believes Musk throttled Starshield at the request of U.S. officials, though the world's richest man has denied any role and said it's the U.S. government that controls the military-grade network. President Trump has also denied he's responsible for slowing the network.
However, CBS News reported Tuesday that Musk was behind the disruption, which occurred after he spoke with administration officials multiple times seeking clarity on the president's thinking on the matter, according to sources familiar with the situation.
There has also been conflicting information about whether full access to the networks has been restored. As of Wednesday afternoon, Starlink remained throttled, Zelenskyy's office confirmed.

item.title: Rising tension on the Korean border fuels concern
item.description:
Tension on the Korean Peninsula is once again ratcheting up, with calls for immediate talks between North and South Korea to avert an accidental military confrontation.
It follows hostile back-to-back statements from Kim Yo Jung – the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un – who said loudspeakers broadcasting anti-South Korea propaganda would be activated within days along the entire 160-mile border.
She also warned Seoul of "the most horrible and distressing situation" if South Korea continues what Pyongyang called interference in North Korean internal affairs.
"This is not a threat," she said, "but a clear warning."
On Wednesday, Kim Yo Jung joined senior military officials to visit fortification sites along the border, where she said North Korean tactical units had taken up positions. She accused South Korean forces of broadcasting warning messages and firing warning shots at multiple locations near the border.
South Korea acknowledged that its forces had fired warning shots, calling them "legitimate and defensive measures."
North Korea expert Bob Carlin, a former U.S. State Department analyst who took part in negotiations with Pyongyang and has followed the country closely for four decades, told CBS News that Kim's statements about "tactical units" are a cause for concern.
"Whether these have heavy weaponry or not, this represents a change in the situation along the front," said Carlin. "Kim Yo Jung also spoke of the possibility of 'deploying more tactical strike means.' This sounds more like artillery and battlefield missile units, and if the decision has been made to move these up, it will be an even more serious change along the front lines."Is China worried that North Korea wants "to confront the U.S."?

item.title: U.K. interests in the Arctic are vulnerable to Russia, lawmakers warn
item.description:
"Glaring gaps" in the United Kingdom's Arctic defenses are leaving it and NATO vulnerable to attacks from Russia, British lawmakers said in a parliamentary report published Thursday.
The group urged the British government to "urgently address" gaps in maritime forces, particularly with the U.S. acting "more unilaterally in the region."
"This is a demanding, hostile environment, and one that our greatest adversary, Russia, is seeking to dominate for military advantage," Tan Dhesi, Chair of the Commons Defense Committee, wrote.
The committee said that a "shockingly low availability" of Royal Navy submarines and warships means critical infrastructure, such as underwater cables and energy supplies, are exposed to potential Russian attacks.
"Russia can then use the ice to conceal and protect its own submarines while threatening NATO sea lanes, U.K. critical infrastructure and the U.K.'s nuclear deterrent," the report added.
The report urged Canada and European NATO allies to "take more responsibility for defence of their interests in the High North."
Like European NATO countries, the United Kingdom lacks "some critical military capabilities that it has largely relied on the U.S. to provide, such as ballistic missile defence, long range strike and intelligence and surveillance assets, which will take considerable investment and time to replicate."
"If the U.K. is to lead an effective coalition," the report continued, "it must address glaring gaps in the availability of its current maritime forces and ensure it has an agreed plan, integrated with European allies in the region, to deter and, if necessary, defeat any aggression in the High North from 2030."
'To deter war we must be ready for it'
Former British Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer warned in June that Russia could attack NATO countries by the end of the decade.

item.title: Son of Stephen Hubbard, American freed from Russian jail, speaks out
item.description:
Washington — Fr. Joseph Coleman feared he would never again see his father, Stephen Hubbard, when they had a brief phone conversation last year while Hubbard was in a Russian prison.
"He was expressing a very extreme tiredness with life, the life that he was experiencing at that time. I don't want to say suicidal thoughts, but the conversation hinted it leaned in that direction," Coleman, a Greek Orthodox priest, told CBS News on Wednesday in his first television interview since his father's release.
Hubbard's release was announced earlier Wednesday during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Hubbard, a U.S. citizen, was imprisoned in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine. The U.S. government had deemed Hubbard wrongfully detained.
Hubbard touched down back in the U.S. Wednesday night, President Trump said while returning from a rally in South Carolina. He said Hubbard would visit the White House "in the next day or so."
Mr. Trump said Putin had agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said that his decision to waive new sanctions against Russia played a role in Hubbard's release.
In a one-minute phone call with his father before Hubbard took off from St. Petersburg, Coleman said he sounded better than he had during their last conversation in May 2025. Witkoff was also present, leaving little opportunity for a private exchange.
"I want to embrace him as a son embraces his father. I want to personally assess his health to make sure he's well," Coleman said. He said he would also give his dad space to adjust to freedom and expected to see Hubbard later that evening.
Coleman, who lives in Cyprus, did not grow up in the same home as Hubbard, who was divorced from Coleman's mother. He said the family had lost track of Hubbard entirely for roughly three years after his detention.

item.title: American Stephen Hubbard released by Russia, Trump confirms
item.description:
Stephen Hubbard, a U.S. citizen who was jailed in Russia for more than four years after being accused of fighting for Ukraine, has been released from custody, President Trump confirmed Wednesday. The release was announced during a meeting between U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
President Trump said in social media posts that Putin agreed to release Hubbard at his request, with "no 'swap' necessary," though he also said the American would not have been released had the White House not stopped new sanctions against Russia from taking effect last week.
Hubbard touched down back in the U.S. Wednesday night, President Trump said while returning from a rally in South Carolina. He said Hubbard would visit the White House "in the next day or so."
The news came as Trump administration officials, including Witkoff, were in St. Petersburg for talks with Putin and other senior Russian officials focused on the Ukraine war.
Video of the meeting showed Witkoff thanking Putin for freeing the American — whom the U.S. government had declared wrongfully detained — and offering the Russian autocrat, who ordered the ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine almost five years ago, effusive praise, including calling him "a humanitarian."
